as_told.title: Mellon and Elizondo bring three Navy videos to the Times

plain: In 2017, Michels says, Luis Elizondo, who ran a small Pentagon office that studied unexplained aerial reports, tried to brief Defense Secretary Jim Mattis on UFOs and was blocked by officials in between. So Elizondo and his friend Christopher Mellon, a former deputy assistant secretary of defense for intelligence, went off script and got three UFO videos cleared for public release by the Pentagon. They brought the videos to the journalist Leslie Kean, and they ran in the New York Times, a source people trusted. Michels names them: the Tic Tac, after a white oval object shaped like the mint, along with Go Fast and Gimbal. He stresses that Navy intelligence had never before admitted the videos were real. A lawyer named Dan Sheehan says the release was fully authorized, cleared by the Defense Department's Office of Prepublication and Security Review, the office that approves material for publication, and dates the front-page story to December 17, 2017. The skeptic Michael Shermer tells it differently, as the moment the government said UAPs, its term for UFOs, are real and Elizondo repeated that the government says so. Either way, it is told as the moment official footage of unknown objects went public.
